title: stt: guard the archive against two concurrent runs of the same file
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The cache lookup and the run-directory write are unlocked. Two processes both miss the cache, both transcribe, and both write the same transcript.json and the same archived audio. Atomic renames keep either file from being torn, but the work is done twice and the loser's rendered outputs can end up beside the winner's transcript.

## User impact
Running the same command in two terminals, or a script that fans out over a folder containing one recording twice, costs double GPU time and can leave rendered files that do not match the stored transcript.

## Cost of inaction
The race stays silent — nothing errors, the transcript looks fine, and the wasted work and the mismatch are visible only to someone comparing files by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Two stt processes transcribing the same file with the same settings never both write the same run directory: one claims the run, the other waits for it or reports the reuse.
- [ ] A multiprocess contention test starts two runs on one file and asserts the transcript is written once and the rendered outputs match it.
- [ ] A crashed or killed holder does not leave the run permanently locked.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: stt: reconcile rig.yaml GitHub settings with the CI workflows it ships

title: stt mic: live dictation that types into the focused field
body:
## What
A new subsystem, not a flag: stt mic listens to the microphone, transcribes continuously with a sliding window, and types the result straight into whatever text field has focus, correcting the last words in place as the decoder changes its mind. A menu-bar icon shows that it is listening, a global hotkey starts and stops it, and a notification confirms each state change. The dictionary applies here as it does everywhere else.

## Why (motivation)
It is in the original request for this tool and is the only part of it that is still missing. Dictation is also the case where the terminology dictionary pays off most: the words a speech model gets wrong are product and project names, and those are exactly the words typed most often into a chat or an editor.

## User impact
Instead of recording a voice memo, waiting, and pasting the result, a person speaks and the words appear where they are already working.

## Cost of inaction
The tool stays a batch transcriber. Every quick thought still costs a recording, a transcription and a paste, which is enough friction that people go on typing instead.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Speaking into the microphone puts text into the focused field of any application within about a second of the words being said, without the user touching stt again.
- [ ] Text already typed is corrected in place when the sliding window revises it, rather than being appended twice.
- [ ] A menu-bar icon appears while listening and disappears when it stops; a global hotkey toggles the mode from any application.
- [ ] pyobjc is an optional extra, exactly like the diarization one: a machine without it keeps every other command working and is told what to install.
- [ ] The model used for live decoding is fast enough for the latency target (whisper.cpp's own streaming example is the starting point, with a small quantized model rather than large-v3-turbo).

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body:
Shipped in [PR #26](https://github.com/alex-mextner/stt-cli/pull/26), merged 2026-09-04, released as 0.3.0.

`stt mic` opens the microphone and types what you say into whatever window has focus. Two models run at once: a fast one answers in about forty milliseconds so words appear while they are still being spoken, and `large-v3-turbo` replaces them a second later with the version that has the proper nouns and the punctuation right. The terminology dictionary reaches both.

Any key you press yourself stops stt correcting the sentence in flight, and it never deletes a character it did not type; a double Escape ends the session.

`stt mic --check` is the answer to "nothing happened": it opens the microphone, draws what it hears against the bar it has to clear, and names which of four causes it was — a permission never granted, the wrong device open, a voice too quiet, or a room mistaken for one.

472 tests. Still open and deliberately not in this: #13 (underlined provisional text), #14 (an always-visible indicator), #21 (subcommands and a hotkey).

**Not closing this yet — two of its five acceptance criteria are genuinely unmet.**

Met:
- Speaking puts text into the focused field of any application within about a second, without touching stt again.
- Text already typed is corrected in place rather than appended twice.
- The live decoding is fast enough for the latency target — though not the way this ticket guessed: instead of one small quantized model, a fast draft model answers in about forty milliseconds and `large-v3-turbo` replaces it a second later. That buys the accuracy the single-small-model plan would have given up.

Not met:
- **A menu-bar icon while listening, and a global hotkey.** Neither shipped. The icon needs an `NSApplication` event loop inside the process, which is a real amount of machinery; it is #14. The hotkey and the daemon that makes it possible are #21.

Not applicable:
- **pyobjc as an optional extra.** There is no pyobjc dependency to make optional: the four macOS calls are reached through `ctypes` against frameworks the system already ships, so this requirement dissolved rather than being satisfied.

This stays open until #14 and #21 land.

title: stt dict check: accept --dict-similarity so it explains the run the user actually made
body:
## What
Give stt dict check the same --dict-similarity option the transcription command takes, defaulting to the configured value. Today the check reads the threshold only from the config file.

## Why (motivation)
The command exists to explain a decision, so it has to be able to run the decision that was actually made. Two other disagreements of exactly this kind were fixed while building the dictionary: the check reimplementing the screen instead of calling it, and the check skipping the threshold validation the pipeline performs.

## User impact
A person who runs a transcription with a lowered threshold, sees an unexpected flag and goes to the check for an explanation currently gets an answer computed at a different threshold, which contradicts the transcript in front of them.

## Cost of inaction
The command meant to remove confusion produces it, and only for people who have already gone out of their way to tune the threshold.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] stt dict check "<line>" --dict-similarity 0.7 reports exactly the flags a transcription run with --dict-similarity 0.7 would produce for that line.
- [ ] With no option given, the command keeps reading the configured value, so nothing changes for anyone who has not asked for anything.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: Give the settled per-run state a type of its own, instead of reusing Settings
body:
## What
Introduce a small ResolvedRun record holding the state the pipeline settles before it computes a cache key — the settings, the dictionary snapshot, the resolved engines, the cross-checks and the recorded engine shortfalls — and pass that one object through the pipeline instead of threading five values into ten-parameter signatures. Settings goes back to meaning what the user asked for.

## Why (motivation)
The load-bearing rule of the caching design is that anything changing the words is settled before the fingerprint is computed, and that rule is currently enforced only by the order in which functions happen to be called. Three separate review rounds named this as the shape the code is drifting toward, and the last change added five settled values, each of which widened four signatures.

## User impact
Nobody sees a difference the day this is done. It protects people from the failure it prevents: asking for a transcription and getting back an old one that was made under different settings — the same words returned again and again no matter what you change, with nothing on screen to say why.

## Cost of inaction
The next setting added widens the same signatures again, and the guarantee that a stored transcript matches the settings it is filed under keeps resting on people remembering the right call order. When that slips, someone gets a wrong transcript served from the archive forever and has no way to tell.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Settings no longer carries fields the pipeline computes (dict_digest, engine_limits, context_compare_chosen); those live on the settled record.
- [ ] The functions that currently take settings plus terms plus backend plus checks plus limits take the settled record instead, and the positional call sites lose their ordering hazard.
- [ ] The existing drift tests keep passing untouched, and the fingerprint of a default run is unchanged, so no archived transcript is invalidated by the refactor.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: Move the shared similarity default to a leaf module so config stops importing dictionary
body:
## What
DEFAULT_SIMILARITY lives in dictionary.py and config.py imports it at module level, while dictionary.py reaches back into config from inside function bodies. Move the constant to a leaf location (config itself or a small constants module) so the dependency runs the way every other module in the package runs it.

## Why (motivation)
There is no cycle today only because every config import inside dictionary.py is deferred into a function body, and nothing in that file says so. The obvious tidy-up — hoisting those imports to the top — breaks the package at import time, in a file that looks unrelated to configuration.

## User impact
Nobody notices this until it breaks, and then it breaks completely: the command stops starting at all, with an error naming a file that has nothing to do with what the person was doing.

## Cost of inaction
The trap stays armed for whoever tidies imports next, and the failure it produces is a tool that will not start rather than a small mistake.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] config.py no longer imports dictionary at module level, and dictionary.py can import config at the top of the file without an ImportError.
- [ ] The threshold is still written down once, and the test tying the fingerprint table, the Settings default and the dictionary default together still passes.

## Screenshots

title: Run speaker diarization end to end on a real recording
body:
## What
stt login unblocked the gated pyannote models, but --diarize has still never been run on an actual multi-speaker recording. Install the extra, run it on a real conversation, and check the speaker labels and the -f speakers dialogue output against what was said.

## Why (motivation)
Everything about this feature has been exercised by tests with the engine mocked out. The one thing nobody has done is run it: the models were gated, so the path stopped at the login step, and the login is the part that just got built.

## User impact
Somebody turns on speaker labels for a meeting recording and finds out only then whether the feature works at all, on a file they cared about.

## Cost of inaction
The feature is advertised in the README and has never once produced a label on real audio. The first person to find out is the person who needed it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A real two-or-more-speaker recording is transcribed with --diarize and the labels follow the actual turns rather than being assigned at random.
- [ ] stt <file> -f speakers produces a readable dialogue transcript from that same recording.
- [ ] Whatever the run turns up — wrong labels, a missing dependency, a crash on a long file — is written down as its own ticket rather than left in a terminal.

title: Add Ollama as a local provider for the LLM correction pass
body:
## What
The --fix pass currently talks to hosted providers. Add Ollama as one more provider so the correction and summary passes can run against a model on the machine, chosen the same way the others are.

## Why (motivation)
It was named in the original request alongside the other providers and is the only one still missing. It is also the only option that keeps a recording on the machine end to end, which for a private conversation is the difference between using the correction pass and not using it.

## User impact
A person transcribing something they do not want to send anywhere can still get the correction pass, instead of choosing between privacy and a readable transcript.

## Cost of inaction
Anyone who cares where their recordings go has to leave --fix switched off, which is the pass that fixes casing, punctuation and the names the decoder guessed wrong.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] stt <file> --fix runs against a local Ollama model with no API key anywhere and no network request leaving the machine.
- [ ] A machine without Ollama running gets the same diagnosed error every other missing dependency produces, naming what to start.
- [ ] The provider choice is part of the run's identity, so a transcript corrected by one model is not served from the archive when another is asked for.

title: stt mic: show provisional text underlined, the way Apple's dictation does
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
stt types its first guess as ordinary characters and then deletes and retypes them when the better answer arrives. That works everywhere, but the user cannot tell which words are settled and which are about to change under them, and the rewrite is visible as a flicker. Apple's own dictation solves this by marking provisional text with an underline. Only an input method can do that: marked text is drawn by the receiving application's text system, and asking for it requires being registered with the system as an input source. That means a small InputMethodKit application installed into ~/Library/Input Methods, which stt would talk to instead of synthesising keystrokes.

## User impact
You can see at a glance which words the computer is still unsure about, instead of watching your own sentence rewrite itself and not knowing whether it has finished.

## Cost of inaction
Live dictation keeps looking slightly unreliable even when it is right, because there is no way to tell a guess from a final answer until it stops changing.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] While a sentence is still being guessed at, the text in the field is visibly marked as provisional (underlined) rather than looking like text the user typed
- [ ] When the accurate pass replaces it, the marking disappears and the text becomes ordinary committed text
- [ ] It works in TextEdit, a browser text field and one Electron application, or the ones it does not work in are listed in the README
- [ ] Installing it is one command and uninstalling it is one command

(none)

title: stt mic: an always-visible indicator that the microphone is open
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Today the state lives in the terminal status line, plus a sound and a notification at the two moments the microphone opens and closes. That is enough to know it started, and not enough to know it is still running twenty minutes later when the terminal is behind three other windows. A menu bar item is the obvious answer and needs an NSApplication event loop running inside the process, which is why it was not built with the rest: it is an application, not a flag. macOS does show its own orange recording indicator, which is a partial substitute and is not specific to stt.

## User impact
You can see at a glance whether the microphone is still open, instead of finding out because a sentence you said to somebody else appeared in a chat window.

## Cost of inaction
A dictation session left running is invisible until it types something, which is exactly the situation where you did not want it typing.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] While dictation is running there is a visible indicator outside the terminal that says whether stt is listening
- [ ] Clicking it offers at least stop, so a session can be ended without finding the terminal it was started from
- [ ] It disappears when dictation ends, including when dictation ends because it failed

title: stt mic: keep a dictation session in the archive, if you ask for it
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Everything stt transcribes from a file goes into the archive, so it can be re-rendered later without touching the GPU. Dictation deliberately does not: it prints the transcript when the session ends and keeps nothing. That default is right, because storing every dictation session means storing a recording of everything you have said at your desk. But there are sessions worth keeping — dictating a document, a long note — and right now the only copy is whatever ended up in the window.

## User impact
You can dictate something long, and still have it if the window it went into gets closed without saving.

## Cost of inaction
Anything dictated exists only in whatever application received it, so one misplaced window closes the only copy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A flag makes stt mic store the session's audio and final text in the archive the same way a transcribed file is stored
- [ ] Without that flag nothing from a dictation session is written to disk beyond what was typed

body:

## Why (motivation)
stt --fix already corrects a transcribed file with an installed agent CLI, and that pass is where the remaining Russian punctuation and casing mistakes get fixed. Dictation stops at the accurate speech model. The machinery for a third, slower pass replacing text in place already exists — it is what the accurate pass does to the draft — so this is mostly wiring plus a decision about how long a wait is acceptable.

Dictated text comes out closer to something you would send without editing it.

## Cost of inaction
Everything dictated still needs a read-through for punctuation, which is most of the time dictation was supposed to save.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A flag makes the LLM correction pass run over each finished sentence and replace it in place, the same way the accurate model replaces the draft

title: stt mic: try Apple's own speech recognition as the fast draft model
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The draft pass exists to be fast and is allowed to be wrong, which is exactly the shape Apple's own recognition fits: it is on-device, supports Russian, streams partial results, and needs no model download at all — so the first run of stt mic would not require a base model. It is unusable as the ACCURATE pass because its Russian punctuation is poor, which is the whole reason stt exists rather than using the system dictation. Reaching it means pyobjc, which is why it is not in the first version: stt has no required third-party dependencies and this would be the first optional one that a core feature reaches for.

## User impact
stt mic would start working immediately after install, without downloading a second speech model first.

## Cost of inaction
Live dictation needs two models on disk before it does anything, which is a slow first experience for a feature whose whole point is being instant.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A measurement of Apple's on-device recognition against base on the same Russian audio: latency, and how wrong the words are
- [ ] Either it becomes an option for the draft pass with the pyobjc it needs as an optional extra, or the measurement is written down and the idea closed

title: stt: both lock files can be replaced out from under the process holding them
body:
Two lock files, one weakness each, and they should be fixed together because the fix is the same shape.

**`dictionary.json.lock`** is opened with `lock.open("a")` and then flocked. If something that is not a regular file is sitting at that path, the open blocks (a named pipe with no reader) or raises out of the middle of the command (a directory). `config.save_setting` had exactly this and now opens its lock non-blocking and asks the descriptor what it is before locking it; the dictionary's copy predates that and was left alone rather than widening a pull request about something else.

**Both locks** protect an inode, not a pathname. If another process unlinks the lock file while one writer holds it, a second writer's `os.open(..., O_CREAT)` creates a fresh inode at the same path and locks that instead — two writers, two different locks, both believing they have exclusive access, and whichever renames last discards the other's setting. The standard fix is to compare `os.fstat(descriptor)` against `os.stat(path)` after acquiring the lock and retry when the inode has moved.

Neither is reachable without another process writing into the application-support folder, which is why they were not fixed inline. Both are cheap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A named pipe or a directory at either lock path produces a diagnosed error rather than hanging or a traceback
- [ ] A lock file replaced while a writer holds it is detected rather than silently producing two exclusive holders
- [ ] There is a test for each shape, on both locks, and each was checked by removing the fix and watching it fail

## Why this matters

`stt dict add` and `stt config set` are the two commands that rewrite a whole file from a copy they read a moment earlier. That is only safe while the lock actually excludes, and right now it stops excluding if the lock file itself is disturbed.

## User impact

Neither command can hang with nothing on screen, or quietly throw away a setting you just made, because of something odd sitting in the application-support folder.

## Cost of not doing it

The locks read as protection and are not, in the two situations somebody would actually go looking for them.

title: stt mic: managed-service subcommands and a configurable hotkey
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Alex asked for the same shape the review dashboard and spec-web already have, so every long-running tool in the ecosystem is driven the same way. The shared library is at agent-tools/lib/agenttools_service.

## User impact
Dictation becomes a key you press from any application, instead of a terminal session you have to keep alive and remember to stop.

## Cost of inaction
stt mic stays a foreground demo: every use costs a terminal window and a manual start, so it does not get used.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A bare 'stt mic' prints help and launches nothing; the six lifecycle subcommands behave as the shared service library defines them (pidfile, launchd autostart, XDG state and cache paths), matching the review dashboard
- [ ] A background daemon idles until a hotkey toggles dictation; the hotkey is settable in config and by flag, and its default is stated in the help text
- [ ] 'stt mic --help' explains the two-pass correction, where the log and pidfile live, which macOS permissions are needed, and what to do when nothing appears
- [ ] Starting dictation is instant: with the daemon running, the delay between the hotkey and the microphone being live is under a second, because both models are already loaded. Measured today, a cold 'stt mic' spends 30-45 seconds loading large-v3-turbo and base before it can hear anything, which is the single largest obstacle to using it

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: no external entities are referenced; the shared library is named by repo path in the motivation

comments.body:
## Design, before writing any of it

### The command surface

```
stt mic                bare: prints help, launches nothing
stt mic once           one dictation session in this shell — exactly what `stt mic` does today
stt mic run            the daemon in the FOREGROUND: models loaded, waiting for the hotkey
stt mic start|stop     the daemon in the background (pidfile)
stt mic status         running? pid, hotkey, models, permissions
stt mic enable|disable OS autostart (launchd), and start/stop now
stt mic check          open the microphone and report whether it hears you
stt mic devices        list microphones
```

`once` exists so today's behaviour keeps a name rather than disappearing; the bare command
becoming help follows `review dashboard`, which is the shape this ticket asked for.

### Why the hotkey cannot be deferred to a later slice

A daemon without one would load the models and then dictate continuously into whatever has
focus, which is not a feature. The lifecycle subcommands and the hotkey are one deliverable.

### How the hotkey is detected

The event tap already watches key-downs, mouse-downs and its own disabling. A modifier
double-tap needs one more event type — `flagsChanged` — plus `CGEventGetFlags`, because the
distinction between left and right Command lives in the device-dependent bits
(`0x8` left, `0x10` right), not in the general `Command` mask.

Default: **double-tap Right Command**, no other key in between, within about 400 ms. It is a
key nothing else binds, it matches the shape of Apple's own Fn-Fn, and it cannot collide with
a shortcut in the focused application. Configurable, with the default stated in `--help`.

### The dependency, and what happens without it

`agenttools_service` is in-ecosystem (`agent-tools/lib/`), not on PyPI, so it cannot be a
plain dependency — `pip install stt-cli` would break on a path that only exists on one
machine. It follows review-cli's pattern: an empty extra with a comment, a lazy import, and
an actionable error naming the editable install when a lifecycle subcommand is used without
it. `once`, `check`, `devices` and bare help must keep working on a machine that lacks it.

title: stt dict learn: build the terminology dictionary from what Alex already writes
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The dictionary is what makes dictation spell project names correctly, and filling it by hand is the reason it stays empty. Alex asked for a fast way to seed it from real usage.

## User impact
Dictated text comes out with the right spelling of the words only this team uses, from the first session, without anyone typing a word list.

## Cost of inaction
The dictionary stays nearly empty, so every dictated project name has to be corrected by hand and the feature is worth little.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] 'stt dict learn' proposes terms mined from sources that already exist on the machine: shell history, git commit subjects and bodies across the checkouts under the work root, and identifiers in code
- [ ] A candidate is offered only when it is frequent, appears across more than one source or day, and is absent from general word lists; each proposal shows where it was seen so it can be judged
- [ ] Typos are not learned: a candidate within a small edit distance of a much more frequent term is treated as a misspelling of it and offered as a correction rule rather than as a word
- [ ] Nothing is written without confirmation; the run is repeatable and does not re-propose what was already rejected
- [ ] A term the speech model gets audibly close but textually wrong is corrected to the spelling in use: dictating the project name that whisper renders as ConLock or ConLoca produces conloca, because the learned dictionary carries the real spelling and the phonetic match reaches it

title: stt: transcribe the macOS Voice Memos library
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Alex asked for this. Voice Memos is where recordings made away from the laptop end up, they sync from the iPhone through iCloud, and today getting one into stt means finding the file by hand in a Group Containers path nobody remembers.

## User impact

## Cost of inaction
Recordings made on the phone stay outside the tool: the user exports them by hand or does not transcribe them at all.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] stt can list the recordings held by the macOS Voice Memos app, showing each one's title, date and length, without the user hunting for the folder it keeps them in
- [ ] A recording is transcribed by name or by selection, and repeat runs reuse the archive rather than decoding the same audio twice
- [ ] New recordings can be transcribed in a batch: a run picks up whatever has appeared since the last one and says what it did
- [ ] The library is only ever READ. Nothing writes to it, renames anything in it, or touches the iCloud sync state, and the help says so plainly, because these are recordings that also live on the user's phone
- [ ] A missing or permission-refused library is reported as a sentence naming what to grant, not as an empty list or a traceback

comments.body:
**Before this can be built, the library layout has to be seen on a machine that has one.**

Checked here: `~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.VoiceMemos.shared` exists but is **empty** — no `Recordings` directory, no database, no audio. So either this Mac has never used Voice Memos, or its recordings have not synced down.

That matters because the interesting part of this ticket is not reading an `.m4a`; it is knowing which file is which recording. Voice Memos keeps titles, dates and folder membership in a CoreData store beside the audio, and the audio filenames are not the titles the user sees. Writing that reader against a remembered schema rather than an observed one would be a guess, and a guess about a database whose files also live on the user's phone.

First step is therefore: record one memo on this Mac (or let iCloud sync one down), then read the actual layout — directory, database filename, and the columns that map a row to a file. Only then design the command.

title: stt diarize: run pyannote the way mlx already runs, instead of installing into the system Python
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The install is broken on this machine and the repo already contains the pattern that fixes it: stt_cli/backends/mlx.py runs its heavy dependency through 'uv run --with mlx-whisper python' in a worker subprocess, needing no install and no virtualenv management. Speaker diarization becomes installable at all on a standard Homebrew setup, and stops being able to damage the user's system Python.

'stt diarize install' fails on any machine using Homebrew Python, which is most of them, and the only ways forward are flags that PEP 668 exists to discourage.

- [ ] 'stt diarize install' succeeds on a machine whose Python is Homebrew's, which refuses installation into itself under PEP 668 — the failure Alex hit
- [ ] Nothing is installed into any interpreter the user did not create: the heavy wheels live in an environment uv builds and caches, exactly as the mlx backend already does with 'uv run --with'
- [ ] 'stt diarize status' reports readiness by asking the environment that will actually run the work, not by importing into the current interpreter
- [ ] A machine without uv is told what to do in one sentence naming the command, rather than shown a page of pip advice

title: Disable leftover SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW via committed .ship-config
body:
## What
GitHub itself does not require an approving review on https://github.com/alex-mextner/stt-cli: classic branch protection is absent (HTTP 404) and there is no ruleset. gh ship still refuses a zero-review PR because the external-review gate defaults ON. The machine-wide off-switch env SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 is ignored after https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/624 — durable disable is a SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 line in the repo-root .ship-config already merged to the PR base (https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/600, https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/609). stt-cli origin/main has no .ship-config. Precedent: https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/commit/17431bf446dffd76016cf84704773a91806e93ba (.ship-config SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0, https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/issues/330) and merged https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/451.

## Why (motivation)
gh ship refuses zero-GitHub-review PRs on https://github.com/alex-mextner/stt-cli even though GitHub branch protection does not require reviews. Env SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 is ignored after https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/624. The documented, audited off-switch is a committed repo-root .ship-config SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 on the PR base branch.

## User impact
When you try to merge a stt-cli PR with gh ship, the command refuses even though GitHub's merge button does not require an approval. You have to post a dummy GitHub review or wait for a Telegram hatch, so a solo ship that already passed review-cli quorum still cannot land.

## Cost of inaction
Every future stt-cli ship stays blocked on a GitHub-side review that the repo policy already turned off, or burns a live Telegram hatch per PR.

- [x] https://github.com/alex-mextner/stt-cli origin/main has a committed repo-root .ship-config whose only ship-gate line is SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 — forced: No UI: criterion 1 proven by 'git show origin/main:.ship-config' = SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 (verified 2026-09-09); criterion 2 proven pre-merge via GitHub branch protection API (HTTP 404, no rulesets) recorded in PR #39's body, unchanged since (no repo-settings-touching PR merged after #39).
